citations.quote: **Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of $\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for $n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and $k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$. **English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is $$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$ where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns** rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row $i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries $$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$ nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row $i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$ and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram. **Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is $$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$ the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$ for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and $[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$: for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$, $$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$ Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty. Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because $\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length $\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus $\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions. **Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is $S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every $n\ge 0$, and we fix $$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$ the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

u\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with $$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$ such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A point $y
otin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $
u\vdash n+1$ with $$[
u]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$ again $
u$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and $\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes of $\lambda$. Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$. A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node $(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node $(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or $\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of $[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately below it. For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so $\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while $\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition of $n\ge0$ with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ and conjugate partition $\lambda'$, whose $j$-th part is the number $\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ in column $j$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $j\ge1$ let $$z_j(\lambda):=\#\{\,i:\lambda_i=j\,\}$$ be the multiplicity with which the positive integer $j$ occurs as a part of $\lambda$; only finitely many $z_j$ are nonzero. - $\lambda$ is **$p$-regular** when every positive part of $\lambda$ occurs fewer than $p$ times, that is, when $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for every $j\ge1$. - $\lambda$ is **$p$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<p$ for every $i\ge1$, where the sequence is padded by the trailing zeros $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>k$. Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite list for $1\le i\le k$. The empty partition $\varnothing\vdash0$ has no parts and $k=0$, so $z_j(\varnothing)=0<p$ and $0-0=0<p$ for every $j,i\ge1$: it is simultaneously $p$-regular and $p$-restricted for every prime $p$. The two conditions are exchanged by conjugation: **$\lambda$ is $p$-restricted if and only if $\lambda'$ is $p$-regular.** The number of columns of $[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$ is the difference $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ of consecutive parts, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$, so the multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$; the stated equivalence compares the same integers with $p$. The names record two genuinely different label conventions used later on this page: James's modular simple modules $D^\lambda$ are labelled by **$p$-regular** $\lambda$. Dual Specht modules themselves are defined for every partition; their simple heads give the **$p$-restricted** labelling of simple modules, related to the first convention by transposition and a sign twist. Neither class of partitions contains the other in general.

Let $F:=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Q(q)|\lambda\rangle$ be the charge-$0$ part of the Fock space of [[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]], with basis indexed by all partitions and with the node operators $F_i,E_i$ defined by the stable finite-prefix action. Assign to $|\lambda\rangle$ the **level-one weight** $$\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle):=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in I}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{cells of }\lambda\text{ of residue }i\},$$ where the **residue** of a cell in row $r$ and column $c$ is $c-r\bmod e$, and the **size** $|\lambda|$ is the separate grading. The vacuum is the empty partition $\varnothing$; $F_i$ adds and $E_i$ removes a node by the explicit finite node formulas of the same item. The toral action is $K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the addable-minus-removable count, proved to be the Cartan pairing in [[lem-the-node-count-is-the-level-one-cartan-pairing]], and $K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$. A partition is **$e$-regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity $<e$, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r\ge1$ (with $\lambda_{r}=0$ beyond the length). These operators are declared linear endomorphisms here; the affine relations proved later establish the actual module structure, so nothing about $F$ is silently assumed in this Definition.

Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite list for $1\le i\le k$. Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that $\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$ ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue $$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$ equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable nodes of residue $i$ ([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]). **The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and $\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$, $\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and $\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are: - the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to the $-$ signs of the reduced signature; - the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes; - the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to the $+$ signs of the reduced signature; - the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal $i$-nodes. Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur, for each residue. **Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence a terminal word is $+^a0^c-^b$ for some $a,b,c\ge0$. The terminal word does not depend on the order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be $0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. A terminating and locally confluent rewriting relation is confluent, so the terminal word is unique; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving $+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature, the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well defined. The empty partition has no $i$-nodes and empty signature, with $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for all $i$. **Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two conventions ([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]], [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form
the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis
suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other
field irreducible summands. The transpose equality

concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use

inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

   counts $\varepsilon_i$, $\varphi_i$ are the numbers of normal and of
   conormal $i$-nodes, and the component is $B(\Lambda_0)$: every $e$-restricted
   shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions.

the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime

classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace

$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is

undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the

formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with

where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and

operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$

is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism

transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.

$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$

in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of

residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the

([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);

characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

Support of the transition polynomials. By [F1] the QG coefficients are $1$ on the diagonal, lie in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ off it, and vanish unless $
u$ is strictly dominated by $\lambda'$ and has the same $e$-core; transporting, $d_{(\lambda,\lambda)} = 1$, the off-diagonal $d_{(\lambda,\mu)}$ lie in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$, and they vanish unless $\mu'$ is strictly dominated by $\lambda'$, equivalently $\mu$ strictly dominates $\lambda$, and $\mu$ shares the $e$-core of $\lambda$. uangle$ occurring in $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda')$ has the same residue multiset as $\lambda'$; transported, $d_{(\lambda,\mu)} 
e 0$ forces $m_j(\mu') = m_j(\lambda')$ for all $j$, that is, the full reflected residue weight of $\mu$ equals that of $\lambda$.

The matrix $H=D^{\mathsf t}D$ is the Gram matrix of the basic lower vectors under the ambient orthonormal form. Since $D(0)$ has distinct coordinate columns, $H(0)=I$ by [F5], proving $\det H\ne0$. The coefficients $e_{(\lambda,\mu)}=(DH^{-1})_{\mu\lambda}$ are in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

The worked instance at $e = 2$. The weight space of $M_{1,1}$ consists of the standard shapes $(2)$ and $(1,1)$ and of the restricted labels $(1,1)$ only, since $(2)$ is not $2$-restricted. By [F4] the QG lower basis has $G(2) = |2\rangle + q|11\rangle$; transposition gives $2' = (1,1)$ and $(1,1)' = 2$, so $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = J^{-1}G(2) = M_{1,1} + qM_2$, whence $D_{\mathrm{rect}} = \binom{q}{1}$ with rows $(2),(1,1)$, $H = D^{\mathsf{t}}D = 1 + q^2$, and $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{qM_2^* + M_{1,1}^*}{1+q^2}$; the coefficient $\frac{1}{1+q^2}$ is not in $A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$, since a Laurent polynomial has no pole at a root of $1+q^2$, so the ambient coordinates are genuinely rational, while the leading term and the integrality of $d$ are as in steps 1.1 and 2.1.

The full ambient dual matrix. On the whole Fock space, $D_{\mathrm{full}}$ is unitriangular by [F1] with off-diagonal entries in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$; its dual basis with respect to the ambient form $B$ has coefficient matrix the transpose inverse $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$, by the same computation as step 2.2 applied to the square unitriangular matrix (here the standard basis of the whole space is orthonormal and the family $\{G(\mu)\}$ is a basis). We claim $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-1}$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$: in every finite truncation the strictly triangular part $N$ of $D_{\mathrm{full}} = 1 + N$ satisfies $N^{m} = 0$ for large $m$, so $(1+N)^{-1} = 1 - N + N^2 - \dots$ is a finite sum with entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$; hence $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$ is Laurent integral, in contrast with the non-integral ambient coordinates of step 3.1.

The exact integral upper basis and the form identification. On the QG standard frame the ambient form is orthonormal. For an addition $\mu=
u+\gamma$ of residue $i$, the node coefficient of $F_i$ is $q^{N_i^r}$, while that of $q^{-1}K_iE_i$ on the reverse edge is $q^{N_i(
u)-1-N_i^l}$. The splitting identity $N_i^r+N_i^l=N_i(
u)-1$ makes them equal ([[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]], [[thm-the-fock-space-node-formulas-satisfy-the-quantum-affine-relations]]). The diagonal toral operators are self-adjoint, and symmetry supplies the reverse $E_i$ identity; thus the ambient form is contravariant for $\sigma(F_i)=q^{-1}K_iE_i$ and $\sigma(E_i)=qF_iK_i^{-1}$. By [F3] the upper bar $\psi^\vee$ fixes each upper basis element, the upper basis comes with its own dual zero and infinity charts whose balanced $\mathbb{Z}$-intersection is the upper lattice, and the upper operators satisfy the exact mixed adjunction with the lower operators, with reductions at $0$ equal to the lower crystal operators; transporting these statements along $J^{-1}$ gives the corresponding upper bar, charts and operators in the symmetric-group convention, distinct from the ordinary lower bar of [F1].

Distinctions and boundary. The construction of steps 1.1 and 2.1 is a **linear** relabelling: $J$ fixes $q$ and only transposes labels, whereas the semilinear involution $|\mu\rangle \mapsto |\mu'\rangle$ of [F4] is the one appearing in adjoint-bar statements, of which LT's symmetry $G^\dagger(\lambda)' = G^-(\lambda')$ is the instance; in particular it does not identify the lower coefficient matrix with its transpose, and by [F1] the equality $d_{\lambda\mu} = d_{\mu'\lambda'}$ for all lower coefficients is false. Finally, the polynomials $d_{(\lambda,\mu)}$ are Fock-space transition coefficients between the standard and lower global bases; identifying them with decomposition numbers of Hecke algebras requires the separate graded/Ariki comparison and the correct Hecke parameter dictionary, which is not asserted here, and every application on this page uses them only as the stated transition data.
